items.prompt:
The three main genres of literature are prose, drama and:

A) Poetry
B) Grammar
C) Rhetoric
D) Syntax

A long narrative work of fiction written in prose is a:

A) Sonnet
B) Novel
C) Sketch
D) Ode

Literature that is written to be performed on stage is:

A) Prose fiction
B) Lyric poetry
C) Drama
D) Epic

A short story that teaches a moral lesson, often using animals, is a:

A) Novel
B) Elegy
C) Memoir
D) Fable

Writing based on real facts and people rather than imagination is:

A) Non-fiction
B) Fiction
C) Fantasy
D) Myth

The sequence of events that make up a story is the:

A) Theme
B) Plot
C) Setting
D) Diction

The time and place in which the events of a story occur is the:

A) Plot
B) Climax
C) Setting
D) Motif

The struggle between opposing forces in a literary work is the:

A) Setting
B) Tone
C) Refrain
D) Conflict

The point of highest tension or turning point in a plot is the:

A) Climax
B) Exposition
C) Prologue
D) Epilogue

The opening part of a plot that introduces characters and background is the:

A) Denouement
B) Exposition
C) Climax
D) Resolution

The final unravelling of the plot after the climax is the:

A) Exposition
B) Prologue
C) Denouement
D) Rising action

A struggle taking place within a character's own mind is called:

A) External conflict
B) Resolution
C) Suspense
D) Internal conflict

A struggle between a character and an outside force is called:

A) External conflict
B) Internal conflict
C) Climax
D) Mood

The part of the plot where complications build tension is the:

A) Falling action
B) Rising action
C) Exposition
D) Denouement

The vantage point from which a story is told is the:

A) Setting
B) Theme
C) Point of view
D) Motif

A narrator who uses 'I' and takes part in the events tells from the:

A) Third-person point of view
B) Editorial view
C) Objective view
D) First-person point of view

A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of all characters is:

A) Omniscient
B) Limited
C) Unreliable
D) First-person

The overall feeling or atmosphere a literary work creates in the reader is the:

A) Plot
B) Mood
C) Setting
D) Rhyme

The writer's attitude towards the subject or audience is the:

A) Mood
B) Theme
C) Tone
D) Climax

The feeling of anxious uncertainty that keeps a reader interested is:

A) Exposition
B) Denouement
C) Diction
D) Suspense

An interruption in a narrative that presents earlier events is a:

A) Flashback
B) Foreshadowing
C) Climax
D) Prologue

A hint that prepares the reader for what will happen later is:

A) Flashback
B) Foreshadowing
C) Resolution
D) Denouement

A choice of words an author uses to express ideas is called:

A) Setting
B) Plot
C) Diction
D) Stanza

A character who changes significantly over the course of a story is a:

A) Static character
B) Flat character
C) Foil
D) Dynamic character

A character who remains essentially unchanged throughout a story is a:

A) Static character
B) Dynamic character
C) Round character
D) Protagonist

A fully developed, complex character is described as:

A) Flat
B) Round
C) Static
D) Minor

A character built around a single dominant trait is described as:

A) Round
B) Dynamic
C) Flat
D) Tragic

The central idea or insight about life conveyed by a literary work is the:

A) Plot
B) Setting
C) Tone
D) Theme

A recurring image, idea or word that runs through a work is a:

A) Motif
B) Climax
C) Stanza
D) Denouement

A narrative in which characters and events stand for abstract ideas is an:

A) Epic
B) Allegory
C) Elegy
D) Ode

When the reader or audience knows something a character does not, it is:

A) Verbal irony
B) Situational irony
C) Dramatic irony
D) Satire

Saying the opposite of what one means for effect is:

A) Dramatic irony
B) Situational irony
C) Paradox
D) Verbal irony

When what happens is the opposite of what is expected, it is:

A) Situational irony
B) Verbal irony
C) Dramatic irony
D) Hyperbole

The use of an object or image to represent a larger idea is:

A) Realism
B) Symbolism
C) Allusion
D) Diction

A play that ends unhappily, often with the downfall of the hero, is a:

A) Comedy
B) Farce
C) Tragedy
D) Masque

A play intended to amuse and which usually ends happily is a:

A) Tragedy
B) Elegy
C) Epic
D) Comedy

A major division of a play into large sections is called an:

A) Act
B) Stanza
C) Canto
D) Verse

A subdivision of an act in a play is a:

A) Stanza
B) Scene
C) Chapter
D) Refrain

The spoken exchange of words between characters in a play is:

A) Narration
B) Stanza
C) Dialogue
D) Diction

A person who performs a part in a play is an:

A) Author
B) Narrator
C) Usher
D) Actor

A long speech in which a character alone on stage reveals inner thoughts is a:

A) Soliloquy
B) Aside
C) Prologue
D) Dialogue

Words a character speaks to the audience that other characters do not hear form an:

A) Soliloquy
B) Aside
C) Epilogue
D) Monologue

A long uninterrupted speech by one character addressed to others is a:

A) Aside
B) Dialogue
C) Monologue
D) Refrain

Introductory lines spoken at the very beginning of a play form the:

A) Epilogue
B) Aside
C) Denouement
D) Prologue

Concluding lines spoken at the end of a play form the:

A) Epilogue
B) Prologue
C) Soliloquy
D) Exposition

Instructions in a play script telling actors how to move or speak are:

A) Footnotes
B) Stage directions
C) Asides
D) Captions

The leading male character in a play is the:

A) Villain
B) Chorus
C) Hero
D) Clown

The leading female character in a play is the:

A) Hero
B) Maid
C) Narrator
D) Heroine

A character who contrasts with another to highlight that character's qualities is a:

A) Foil
B) Hero
C) Chorus
D) Narrator

The error or flaw in a tragic hero that leads to his downfall is the:

A) Climax
B) Tragic flaw
C) Catastrophe
D) Prologue

Excessive pride that brings about a tragic hero's fall is called:

A) Catharsis
B) Hamartia
C) Hubris
D) Nemesis

The release of pity and fear an audience feels at the end of a tragedy is:

A) Hubris
B) Climax
C) Irony
D) Catharsis

A comedy that relies on exaggerated, improbable situations for laughter is a:

A) Farce
B) Tragedy
C) Elegy
D) Sonnet

A play that blends serious themes with a happy ending is a:

A) Pure tragedy
B) Tragicomedy
C) Pure comedy
D) Epic

A drama set to music in which the words are sung throughout is an:

A) Aside
B) Ode
C) Opera
D) Eulogy

A short comic or musical performance between the acts of a play is an:

A) Epilogue
B) Aside
C) Overture
D) Interlude

In classical Greek tragedy, the group that comments on the action in song is the:

A) Chorus
B) Cast
C) Troupe
D) Ensemble

The classical rule that a play should cover one main action, one place and one day is the:

A) Three estates
B) Three unities
C) Three acts
D) Three graces

A play written to be read rather than staged is a:

A) Masque
B) Mystery play
C) Closet drama
D) Farce

A medieval play that teaches morals through personified virtues and vices is a:

A) Mystery play
B) Masque
C) Farce
D) Morality play

A medieval play dramatising stories from the Bible is a:

A) Mystery play
B) Morality play
C) Closet drama
D) Opera

An elaborate court entertainment combining poetry, music and dance is a:

A) Mystery play
B) Masque
C) Farce
D) Interlude

The technique by which the audience knows more than the characters do is:

A) Verbal irony
B) Caricature
C) Dramatic irony
D) Allusion

A play that ridicules folly or vice to bring about reform is a:

A) Tragedy
B) Pastoral
C) Elegy
D) Satire

The rising tension in a play builds towards its:

A) Climax
B) Prologue
C) Exposition
D) Epilogue

A drama centred on the troubles of ordinary people rather than nobility is:

A) Heroic tragedy
B) Domestic tragedy
C) Revenge tragedy
D) Comedy of manners

A comedy that mocks the manners and affectations of a social class is a:

A) Farce
B) Slapstick
C) Comedy of manners
D) Burlesque

A poem of fourteen lines is called a:

A) Ode
B) Ballad
C) Epic
D) Sonnet

A poem that mourns or laments the dead is an:

A) Elegy
B) Ode
C) Epic
D) Idyll

A long narrative poem celebrating heroic deeds is an:

A) Elegy
B) Epic
C) Sonnet
D) Limerick

A poem or song that tells a story, often handed down orally, is a:

A) Ode
B) Sonnet
C) Ballad
D) Eulogy

A short poem expressing personal thoughts and feelings is a:

A) Epic
B) Ballad
C) Saga
D) Lyric

A group of lines forming a unit in a poem is a:

A) Stanza
B) Canto
C) Foot
D) Caesura

A stanza or unit of two lines, usually rhyming, is a:

A) Tercet
B) Couplet
C) Quatrain
D) Octave

A stanza of three lines is a:

A) Couplet
B) Quatrain
C) Tercet
D) Sestet

A stanza of four lines is a:

A) Couplet
B) Tercet
C) Octave
D) Quatrain

The eight-line first section of an Italian sonnet is the:

A) Octave
B) Sestet
C) Couplet
D) Quatrain

The six-line second section of an Italian sonnet is the:

A) Octave
B) Sestet
C) Couplet
D) Tercet

A formal poem of praise addressed to a person, thing or idea is an:

A) Elegy
B) Epic
C) Ode
D) Ballad

A humorous five-line poem with an AABBA rhyme scheme is a:

A) Sonnet
B) Haiku
C) Ballad
D) Limerick

A Japanese three-line poem of seventeen syllables (5-7-5) is a:

A) Haiku
B) Sonnet
C) Limerick
D) Tercet

The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of verse is the:

A) Rhyme
B) Metre
C) Stanza
D) Theme

Poetry written without a regular metre or rhyme scheme is:

A) Blank verse
B) Heroic verse
C) Free verse
D) Doggerel

Unrhymed lines written in iambic pentameter are called:

A) Free verse
B) Couplets
C) Sprung rhythm
D) Blank verse

The repetition of similar sounds at the ends of lines of verse is:

A) Rhyme
B) Rhythm
C) Metre
D) Diction

The fixed pattern of end rhymes in a poem is called the:

A) Metre
B) Rhyme scheme
C) Foot
D) Caesura

A single line of poetry is also referred to as a:

A) Stanza
B) Canto
C) Verse
D) Foot

A deliberate pause or break within a line of poetry is a:

A) Enjambment
B) Refrain
C) Foot
D) Caesura

The running-on of a sentence from one line of verse to the next without a pause is:

A) Enjambment
B) Caesura
C) Refrain
D) Couplet

A line or group of lines repeated at intervals in a poem is the:

A) Caesura
B) Refrain
C) Octave
D) Foot

A metrical foot of one unstressed syllable followed by one stressed syllable is an:

A) Trochee
B) Dactyl
C) Iamb
D) Spondee

A metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by one unstressed syllable is a:

A) Iamb
B) Anapaest
C) Spondee
D) Trochee

A metrical foot of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed one is an:

A) Anapaest
B) Dactyl
C) Iamb
D) Trochee

A metrical foot of two stressed syllables together is a:

A) Iamb
B) Trochee
C) Spondee
D) Dactyl

A line of poetry with five metrical feet is written in:

A) Tetrameter
B) Trimeter
C) Hexameter
D) Pentameter

A line of poetry with four metrical feet is written in:

A) Tetrameter
B) Pentameter
C) Trimeter
D) Hexameter

A line of poetry with six metrical feet is written in:

A) Pentameter
B) Hexameter
C) Tetrameter
D) Trimeter

A sonnet made of three quatrains and a final couplet is the:

A) Petrarchan sonnet
B) Spenserian stanza
C) Shakespearean sonnet
D) Ballad stanza

A sonnet divided into an octave and a sestet is the:

A) Shakespearean sonnet
B) Miltonic ode
C) Ballad
D) Petrarchan sonnet

An elaborate, extended and surprising comparison common in metaphysical poetry is a:

A) Conceit
B) Refrain
C) Caesura
D) Stanza

A prose narrative shorter than a novel but with a full plot is a:

A) Sonnet
B) Short story
C) Stanza
D) Ode

A long fictional narrative written in prose is a:

A) Sonnet
B) Elegy
C) Novel
D) Ballad

The story of a person's life written by that same person is an:

A) Biography
B) Memoir of others
C) Eulogy
D) Autobiography

An account of a person's life written by someone else is a:

A) Biography
B) Autobiography
C) Diary
D) Obituary

A story drawn from the imagination rather than fact is called:

A) Non-fiction
B) Fiction
C) Report
D) Essay

A prose narrative longer than a short story but shorter than a novel is a:

A) Sonnet
B) Saga
C) Novella
D) Fable

The person who tells the story in a work of prose is the:

A) Author
B) Protagonist
C) Editor
D) Narrator

A story told by a character who took part in it uses:

A) First-person narration
B) Omniscient narration
C) Objective narration
D) Editorial narration

A narrator standing outside the story who knows all thoughts is:

A) First-person narrator
B) Omniscient narrator
C) Unreliable narrator
D) Frame narrator

A narrator whose account the reader cannot fully trust is an:

A) Omniscient narrator
B) Objective narrator
C) Unreliable narrator
D) Third-person narrator

A secondary story line that runs alongside the main plot is a:

A) Climax
B) Prologue
C) Refrain
D) Subplot

The background information given at the start of a prose work is the:

A) Exposition
B) Denouement
C) Climax
D) Epilogue

Telling part of a story out of order by returning to earlier events uses a:

A) Foreshadowing
B) Flashback
C) Prologue
D) Refrain

A novel that traces the moral and psychological growth of a young hero is a:

A) Picaresque novel
B) Epistolary novel
C) Bildungsroman
D) Gothic novel

A novel told mainly through letters exchanged between characters is an:

A) Bildungsroman
B) Picaresque novel
C) Historical novel
D) Epistolary novel

A novel with a mysterious, gloomy and frightening atmosphere is a:

A) Gothic novel
B) Pastoral novel
C) Comic novel
D) Detective novel

A novel set in an imagined future or built on scientific ideas is:

A) Historical fiction
B) Science fiction
C) Realism
D) Romance

A brief story that illustrates a moral or religious lesson is a:

A) Saga
B) Sonnet
C) Parable
D) Ode

A short tale, often with animals, that ends with a moral is a:

A) Epic
B) Elegy
C) Ballad
D) Fable

A traditional story explaining natural events, often involving gods, is a:

A) Myth
B) Legend
C) Novella
D) Memoir

A traditional story about heroes, sometimes based on real history, is a:

A) Myth
B) Legend
C) Essay
D) Diary

Conversation between characters reproduced in a prose work is:

A) Monologue
B) Narration
C) Dialogue
D) Exposition

The technique of presenting a character's unbroken flow of thoughts is:

A) Foreshadowing
B) Flashback
C) Allusion
D) Stream of consciousness

A prose work that imitates and mocks the style of another work is a:

A) Parody
B) Parable
C) Pastoral
D) Eulogy

A long prose narrative following the adventures of a roguish hero is a:

A) Gothic novel
B) Picaresque novel
C) Epistolary novel
D) Bildungsroman

A prose work whose surface story carries a deeper symbolic meaning is an:

A) Parody
B) Memoir
C) Allegory
D) Diary

The faithful, detailed representation of everyday life in fiction is:

A) Romanticism
B) Surrealism
C) Allegory
D) Realism

A novel that exposes injustice and the problems of its society is a:

A) Social novel
B) Romance
C) Fairy tale
D) Pastoral

The atmosphere or dominant feeling created in a prose passage is its:

A) Plot
B) Mood
C) Setting
D) Foil

The way an author reveals the personality of the people in a story is:

A) Plotting
B) Versification
C) Characterisation
D) Scansion

An introductory section before the main narrative of a novel is a:

A) Epilogue
B) Caesura
C) Refrain
D) Prologue

A concluding section after the main narrative of a novel is an:

A) Epilogue
B) Prologue
C) Exposition
D) Aside

A daily personal record of events and private thoughts is a:

A) Sonnet
B) Diary
C) Ballad
D) Ode

A story told by 'he' or 'she' from outside the action uses:

A) First-person narration
B) Second-person narration
C) Third-person narration
D) Choral narration

A direct comparison that says one thing is another, without 'like' or 'as', is a:

A) Simile
B) Pun
C) Litotes
D) Metaphor

A comparison of two things using 'like' or 'as' is a:

A) Simile
B) Metaphor
C) Allusion
D) Paradox

Giving human qualities to animals, objects or ideas is:

A) Hyperbole
B) Personification
C) Metonymy
D) Irony

A deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis or effect is:

A) Litotes
B) Understatement
C) Hyperbole
D) Euphemism

Describing one thing by comparing it to another throughout a passage is an:

A) Single simile
B) Short pun
C) Brief allusion
D) Extended metaphor

A figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole is:

A) Synecdoche
B) Metaphor
C) Simile
D) Paradox

Replacing the name of a thing with that of something closely related, e.g. 'the crown' for monarchy, is:

A) Synecdoche
B) Metonymy
C) Simile
D) Litotes

An indirect reference to a well-known person, event or work is an:

A) Illusion
B) Apostrophe
C) Allusion
D) Epithet

A statement that seems self-contradictory yet expresses a truth is a:

A) Pun
B) Simile
C) Euphemism
D) Paradox

Two contradictory words placed side by side, e.g. 'bitter-sweet', form an:

A) Oxymoron
B) Paradox
C) Pun
D) Cliché

A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh or blunt one is a:

A) Hyperbole
B) Euphemism
C) Metaphor
D) Pun

Deliberately representing something as less important than it is, for effect, is:

A) Hyperbole
B) Personification
C) Understatement
D) Apostrophe

An understatement that affirms something by denying its opposite, e.g. 'not bad', is:

A) Hyperbole
B) Oxymoron
C) Pun
D) Litotes

Addressing an absent person or an abstract idea as if it were present is:

A) Apostrophe
B) Allusion
C) Antithesis
D) Metonymy

Setting contrasting ideas against each other in balanced phrasing is:

A) Anaphora
B) Antithesis
C) Apostrophe
D) Allusion

Repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses is:

A) Antithesis
B) Caesura
C) Anaphora
D) Conceit

A humorous play on words that exploits double meanings is a:

A) Paradox
B) Metaphor
C) Simile
D) Pun

A fixed expression whose meaning differs from its literal words, e.g. 'kick the bucket', is an:

A) Idiom
B) Simile
C) Pun
D) Conceit

A widely used, overworked expression that has lost its freshness is a:

A) Conceit
B) Cliché
C) Pun
D) Caesura

A question asked only for effect, not requiring an answer, is a:

A) Direct question
B) Indirect question
C) Rhetorical question
D) Tag question

Reversing the normal order of words for emphasis or rhythm is:

A) Apostrophe
B) Anaphora
C) Allusion
D) Inversion

Describing one sense in terms of another, e.g. 'a loud colour', is:

A) Synaesthesia
B) Onomatopoeia
C) Metonymy
D) Litotes

A descriptive word or phrase regularly attached to a name, e.g. 'swift-footed Achilles', is an:

A) Allusion
B) Epithet
C) Conceit
D) Pun

An adjective shifted from the person it describes to a nearby thing, e.g. 'a sleepless night', is a:

A) Simile
B) Metonymy
C) Transferred epithet
D) Cliché

Comparing two unlike things in an implied way by calling one the other is the basis of the:

A) Pun
B) Litotes
C) Refrain
D) Metaphor

Representing an abstract quality, such as Justice, as a human figure is:

A) Personification
B) Apostrophe
C) Allusion
D) Metonymy

Saying 'I have told you a thousand times' to stress frequency is an example of:

A) Litotes
B) Hyperbole
C) Understatement
D) Euphemism

Calling a very tall man 'Shorty' as a joke is an example of:

A) Metaphor
B) Simile
C) Irony
D) Synecdoche

Using a dove to stand for peace is an example of:

A) Onomatopoeia
B) Antithesis
C) Caesura
D) Symbolism

Calling life 'a journey' is an example of a:

A) Simile
B) Metaphor
C) Pun
D) Litotes

Saying 'the White House announced' to mean the country's leader relies on:

A) Simile
B) Hyperbole
C) Metonymy
D) Paradox

The repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words is:

A) Assonance
B) Consonance
C) Rhyme
D) Alliteration

The repetition of similar vowel sounds in nearby words is:

A) Assonance
B) Alliteration
C) Consonance
D) Onomatopoeia

A word that imitates the natural sound it describes, like 'buzz', is:

A) Alliteration
B) Onomatopoeia
C) Assonance
D) Euphony

The matching of sounds at the ends of two or more lines of verse is:

A) Rhythm
B) Metre
C) Rhyme
D) Diction

The regular recurrence of stressed and unstressed beats in verse is:

A) Rhyme
B) Refrain
C) Diction
D) Rhythm

Saying a word or phrase again for emphasis or musical effect is:

A) Repetition
B) Inversion
C) Allusion
D) Caesura

The repetition of consonant sounds within or at the end of nearby words is:

A) Assonance
B) Consonance
C) Alliteration
D) Onomatopoeia

Rhyme that occurs at the ends of lines of poetry is:

A) Internal rhyme
B) Eye rhyme
C) End rhyme
D) Half rhyme

Rhyme that occurs within a single line of poetry is:

A) End rhyme
B) Eye rhyme
C) Masculine rhyme
D) Internal rhyme

Words that look as if they rhyme in spelling but do not in sound, e.g. 'love'/'move', show:

A) Eye rhyme
B) Internal rhyme
C) End rhyme
D) Perfect rhyme

A line or phrase repeated at regular intervals, especially in songs, is a:

A) Caesura
B) Foot
C) Refrain
D) Stanza

A pleasant, harmonious and smooth arrangement of sounds is:

A) Cacophony
B) Caesura
C) Diction
D) Euphony

A harsh, discordant and unpleasant arrangement of sounds is:

A) Cacophony
B) Euphony
C) Assonance
D) Rhythm

The repetition of soft 's', 'sh' and 'z' sounds to create a hissing effect is:

A) Cacophony
B) Sibilance
C) Consonance
D) Rhyme

Words such as 'hiss', 'crackle' and 'murmur' are examples of:

A) Assonance
B) Consonance
C) Onomatopoeia
D) Euphony

A pause near the middle of a line of verse, often marked by punctuation, is a:

A) Enjambment
B) Foot
C) Refrain
D) Caesura

The carrying of sense and grammar past the end of a verse line without pause is:

A) Enjambment
B) Caesura
C) End-stopping
D) Refrain

A line of verse that ends with a natural pause and punctuation is:

A) Run-on
B) End-stopped
C) Enjambed
D) Caesural

The emphasis placed on certain syllables in a line of poetry is called:

A) Pitch
B) Pause
C) Stress
D) Rhyme

The phrase 'wild and windy weather' is an example of:

A) Assonance
B) Onomatopoeia
C) Rhyme
D) Alliteration

The phrase 'the rain in Spain' repeating the long 'a' sound shows:

A) Assonance
B) Alliteration
C) Consonance
D) Sibilance

The overall musical quality produced by a poem's sounds and rhythm is its:

A) Plot
B) Melody
C) Theme
D) Setting

Rhyme on two syllables where the last is unstressed, e.g. 'mother'/'brother', is:

A) Masculine rhyme
B) Eye rhyme
C) Internal rhyme
D) Feminine rhyme
